newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN has word of new Zaire rebel killings of Rwandans.
newsitem.headline: UN has word of new Zaire rebel killings of Rwandans.

text.p: The U.N. refugee agency voiced concern on Wednesday about reports of fresh killings of Rwandan Hutu refugees in Zaire by Tutsi-dominated rebels in recent days.

Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole said UNHCR had reports from Zairean interior ministry and usually reliable independent sources in Zaire that rebels had killed refugees near Mbandaka town, northeast of the capital Kinshasa on the Zaire river.
"We've had reports of killings of Rwandan Hutu refugees by the rebel alliance soldiers in this area. We can't confirm them because we have no presence there," O'Toole said.
"We are very concerned about the safety of Rwandan Hutu refugees. We're trying to check out these reports," she said.
France, quoting eyewitness reports and reliable sources, on Tuesday accused the rebels of slaughtering refugees after taking Mbandaka and urged an international appeal to stop killings.
O'Toole said the region, where UNHCR had reports of a presence of up to 50,000 Rwandan Hutus, was off-limits to aid workers because of continuing fighting.
The refugees are the rump of two million Rwandan Hutus who fled in fear of reprisal for 1994's Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis.

Aid officials in Geneva fear rebels are hunting down and killing the Hutus to save themselves the trouble and risk of repatriating them to Rwanda, where they are collectively accused of genocide by Tutsi survivors.
More than half a million Rwandan Hutus went home late last year but UNHCR says up to 300,000 remain in Zaire. Rwanda says only 30,000 Hutu refugees are left in Zaire.
UNHCR figures were also challenged as too high by the United States, which has developed close military and political ties with Rwanda's new Tutsi-dominated rulers.
O'Toole said UNHCR believed there were ex-Rwandan army soldiers and Hutu militiamen among the refugees in Mbandaka.
Aid officials in Geneva fear hundreds of refugees may have been killed by the rebels in recent days. They also fear that aid workers may become a target of rebel hostility.
